lessons.title: Inodes, hard links and symbolic links
lessons.goal:
Learn that a file is an **inode** and a name is just an entry in a directory pointing to it, and see the difference between hard and symbolic links.

Why it matters: it explains why deleting a name does not always free space, why `mv` is instant, and why a hard link cannot cross file systems.

setup.note: Steps with sudo mount small RAM file systems (tmpfs) under /tmp/lab and unmount them again.

steps.title: A name points to an inode
steps.text: The **inode** holds everything about a file except its name: owner, mode, size, timestamps and where the data blocks are. A **directory** is a table of names and inode numbers. `ls -i` shows the number.

steps.title: A hard link is a second name
steps.text: `ln a.txt b.txt` adds a second name for the **same inode**. The link count becomes 2. Both names are equal: neither is the "original".

steps.title: Deleting a name
steps.text: `rm` removes one name and decrements the link count. The data is freed only when the count reaches 0 **and** no process has the file open.

run.cmd: rm a.txt; stat -c 'links=%h' b.txt; cat b.txt

steps.title: A symbolic link is a small file with a path
steps.text: `ln -s TARGET LINK` creates a new inode that contains the **path** of the target. It can point to directories and to other file systems, and it can **dangle**: if the target is removed it points to nothing.

run.cmd: rm b.txt; cat s.txt; ls -l s.txt | awk '{print $9, $10, $11}'
run.output:
cat: s.txt: No such file or directory
s.txt -> b.txt

steps.title: Hard links cannot cross file systems
steps.text: An inode number is only unique inside one file system, so a hard link to another file system is refused. A symbolic link works because it stores only a path.

run.output: ln: failed to create hard link '/dev/shm/f.txt' => 'f.txt': Invalid cross-device link

steps.under: `mv` within one file system only changes directory entries (a `rename` system call): the inode number stays the same, so moving a 100 GB file is instant. Across file systems `mv` must copy and delete. `cp` always creates a new inode.

options: A table of names and inode numbers

quiz.q: `ln a b` then `rm a`. What happens to the data?
quiz.explain: The link count dropped from 2 to 1.

quiz.q: Which link type can cross file systems?
Why is `mv` of a huge file inside one file system instant?

check.scenario: You must free 10 GB by deleting a big file, but `df` does not change after `rm`. Name two possible reasons related to this lesson.
check.answer:
1. The file has **another hard link** elsewhere (check `stat -c %h` or `find / -xdev -samefile FILE`), so the inode stays.
2. A running process still has it **open** (see the deleted-but-open lesson), so the blocks are freed when the process closes it.

lessons.title: Disk full, but df shows free space: inodes
lessons.goal:
Learn that a file system has a limited number of inodes, how to reproduce running out of inodes, and how to find the directory that holds the millions of files.

Why it matters: `No space left on device` while `df -h` shows free space is almost always inode exhaustion (or a deleted-but-open file).

setup.note: Steps with sudo mount small RAM file systems (tmpfs) under /tmp/lab and unmount them again.

steps.title: Two separate resources
steps.text: A file system has **blocks** for data and **inodes** for files. Creating a file needs an inode, even if it is empty. With millions of tiny files you run out of inodes long before you run out of blocks. `df -i` shows inode use.

steps.title: A small file system with few inodes
steps.text: We mount a 10 MB RAM file system limited to 50 inodes (`nr_inodes`). Plenty of space, very few inodes.

run.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/small && sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=10m,nr_inodes=50 tmpfs /tmp/lab/small && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/small

steps.title: Create files until it fails
steps.text: Each empty file uses one inode and no data blocks.

run.cmd: for i in $(seq 1 100); do : > /tmp/lab/small/f$i || break; done 2>&1 | tail -n 1
run.output: bash: /tmp/lab/small/f45: No space left on device

steps.title: The symptom and the diagnosis
steps.text: Writing fails with `No space left on device`, but `df -h` still shows free space. `df -i` shows 100% inode use.

run.output: bash: /tmp/lab/small/new.txt: No space left on device

steps.title: Find the directory with too many files
steps.text: Count entries per directory with `find`. On a real server run this on the full file system and look at the top directories (sessions, mail queues and caches are typical).

run.cmd: find /tmp/lab -xdev -maxdepth 2 | cut -d/ -f1-4 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3

steps.under: On **ext4** the number of inodes is fixed when the file system is created (`mkfs.ext4 -N` or `-i bytes-per-inode`). On **xfs** and **btrfs** inodes are allocated dynamically, so exhaustion is rare (xfs can still fail if the free space is too fragmented to allocate inode chunks).

quiz.q: `df -h` shows 40% free, but writes fail with ENOSPC. First suspect?
Does an empty file use an inode?
options: Only if it has a name longer than 8 characters

quiz.q: Which file systems allocate inodes dynamically?
quiz.explain: Unlike ext4, they do not fix the count at mkfs time.

check.scenario: A mail server's /var/spool is out of inodes. You cannot `rm *` (argument list too long). How do you delete the millions of files safely?
check.answer: `find /var/spool/dir -type f -delete` (no argument list, one `unlink` per file) or `rsync -a --delete /empty/ /var/spool/dir/`. Then fix the cause (stuck queue, cleanup job) and consider a separate file system with more inodes for that directory.

lessons.title: Deleted but still open: lsof +L1 and /proc/PID/fd
lessons.goal:
Reproduce a file that was deleted but still takes space, find it, recover its content and free the space without restarting the process.

Why it matters: after rotating or deleting a big log, `df` still says full. This is the classic cause, and `/proc` lets you fix it live.

setup.note: Steps with sudo mount small RAM file systems (tmpfs) under /tmp/lab and unmount them again.

steps.title: Set up the situation
steps.text: A 16 MB RAM file system. We write an 8 MB "log", start a process that holds it open (`sleep` with the file as stdin), and delete the file.

run.cmd: sudo mkdir -p /tmp/lab/disk && sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=16m tmpfs /tmp/lab/disk && sudo chown $(id -un): /tmp/lab/disk

dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/lab/disk/app.log bs=1M count=8 status=none; sleep 600 < /tmp/lab/disk/app.log & echo $! > holder.pid; sleep 0.3; df -h /tmp/lab/disk | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "used before rm:", $3}'
rm /tmp/lab/disk/app.log; ls /tmp/lab/disk | wc -l; df -h /tmp/lab/disk | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "used after rm: ", $3}'

steps.after: The directory is empty, but the 8 MB is still used.

steps.title: du and df disagree
steps.text: `du` walks names, so it sees nothing. `df` asks the file system, so it counts the blocks.

steps.title: Find the holder: lsof +L1
steps.text: `+L1` lists open files whose **link count is below 1**: files with no name left. `+a` limits the list to one file system.

run.output:
COMMAND     PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NLINK NODE NAME
sleep   3467615  opc    0r   REG  0,182  8388608     0    2 /tmp/lab/disk/app.log (deleted)

steps.title: The same fact in /proc
steps.text: Every open descriptor is a link in `/proc/PID/fd`. For a deleted file the link text ends with `(deleted)`, and you can still **read** the file through it.
steps.under: Opening `/proc/PID/fd/N` does not look up a name: it is a magic link that gives you the **same inode** through the process's descriptor. That is why the content can be copied out although the name is gone. The inode is freed when its link count is 0 and its open count is 0.

steps.title: Free the space without restarting
steps.text: If the data is not needed, truncate the file through the same link. The space returns at once and the process keeps running (it holds an empty file). Restarting the process would also free it, but may interrupt a service.

run.cmd: : > /proc/$(cat holder.pid)/fd/0; df -h /tmp/lab/disk | tail -n 1 | awk '{print "used after truncate:", $3}'
kill $(cat holder.pid); sudo umount /tmp/lab/disk; echo cleaned

options: Open files with a link count of zero (deleted)
quiz.explain: Deleted files that are still open.

quiz.q: Why does `du` not see a deleted open file?
options: du walks directory names and the name is gone

quiz.q: How can you read the content of a deleted open file?
quiz.explain: The magic link opens the same inode.

quiz.q: Which action frees the space without stopping the process?

check.scenario: After `logrotate` deleted `app.log.1` (30 GB), `df` still shows 100%. The application must keep running. What do you do?
check.answer: `lsof +L1 /mount` (or `ls -l /proc/*/fd | grep deleted`) to find the process and descriptor. If the data is not needed: `: > /proc/PID/fd/N` frees the space. Better: make the application reopen its log (send the right signal, or restart in a window) and configure logrotate with `postrotate` or `copytruncate` so it does not happen again.

interview.a: The file system object that holds a file's metadata (owner, mode, size, times) and the location of its data. A directory maps names to inode numbers. See [the lesson](#/lesson/18/inodes-links).
A hard link is another name for the same inode (same file system only). A symbolic link is a separate small file that stores a path and can dangle or cross file systems.

interview.q: `df -h` shows free space but you cannot create files. Why?
interview.a: Out of inodes (check `df -i`), or a quota, or a deleted file held open. See [inode exhaustion](#/lesson/18/inode-exhaustion).

interview.q: How do you find deleted-but-open files and free the space?
interview.a: `lsof +L1` or `/proc/PID/fd` links ending in (deleted). Truncate via `: > /proc/PID/fd/N` or restart the process. See [the lesson](#/lesson/18/deleted-but-open).

interview.q: Why is `mv` fast within a file system but slow across file systems?
interview.a: Within one file system it renames a directory entry. Across file systems it must copy the data and delete the source.

interview.q: Why can't hard links cross file systems?
interview.a: An inode number is only meaningful inside its own file system, so a directory entry cannot point to an inode in another one.

glossary.def: The file system record of a file's metadata and data location (not its name).
An additional directory entry pointing to the same inode.
A small file that stores the path of another file.
The number of names (directory entries) that point to an inode.
No free inodes left, so no new files can be created even if blocks are free.
A file with no name left that a process still holds open; its space is not freed yet.

commands.desc: Show inode, links, size and times.
Find all names of one inode.
Delete many files without argument limits.
List deleted files that are still open.
